post:
In interwar Zlín, each Baťa shoe workshop kept its own accounts, and its staff shared its profit and its loss. The Czech name was dílenská samospráva, workshop self-management.

Nadace Tomáše Bati dates the system to 1924. Three rules made it run, according to Czech author Václav Lednický: profit settled each week, rules fixed for each 6-month plan, and shares paid workshop by workshop, whatever the losses elsewhere.

The system did not survive the end of private ownership. The plants were nationalised in 1945, and in 1949 Zlín became Gottwaldov while the plants became the national enterprise Svit.

Its disappearance proves little about the method itself. A regime change removed it, and the sources give no figures on what workers gained or lost each week.

Link to the full article in the comments.
short: Baťa's Zlín workshops each kept their own weekly profit and loss from 1924. Nationalisation ended the system, and its disappearance proves little about the method.
ig: Every workshop kept its own books. From 1924, each Baťa shoe workshop in Zlín ran its own accounts, and its staff shared its profit and its loss, settled every week. The system did not survive nationalisation in 1945 and the new regime that followed. Its disappearance says little about whether it worked, and no firm we know of runs it today.
